title: Model-Based Normal Tissue Complication Probability Comparison Between Proton and Photon Therapies for Brain Tumors Complying With Planning Study Guidelines

license.text: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/).

paragraphs.en: Proton beam therapy (PBT) lowers radiation doses to normal tissues surrounding tumors compared with photon therapy, potentially reducing adverse events, particularly within the complex and delicate structures of the central nervous system (CNS). However, PBT insurance coverage in Japan remains limited because of high costs and few available facilities. In addition, the necessity for prolonged posttreatment follow-up to observe late CNS toxicities, combined with substantial associated costs and rapid technological innovations, severely limits the implementation of randomized controlled trials. The significant costs associated with the extended follow-up make it difficult to conduct studies, and new innovations are likely to render study results of little use.

Normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) is a mathematical model based on the relationship between the prescription dose and adverse events for patients treated with radiation therapy. Langendijk et al1 defined the model-based approach as an attempt to verify the superiority of different treatments by comparing them with NTCP. This approach can show the usefulness of particle therapy for diseases where its benefits have been difficult to verify.

Conventional planning studies often lacked standardized reporting formats and clear definitions for ensuring equivalent tumor dosing, meaning observed NTCP differences could not be attributed purely to the treatment modality itself. Hansen et al2 defined Radiotherapy Treatment plannINg study Guidelines (RATING) as a research framework for radiation therapy treatment planning studies comparing different treatment modalities and techniques. To our knowledge, no previous study comparing PBT and photon therapy has followed this framework,3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and we compared different treatment modalities objectively by using RATING and specific criteria we established to ensure equivalent doses to tumors.

In Japan, all cases treated with PBT after May 2016 are enrolled in a prospective registry study (Proton-net), and the treatment policy is to use the dose division specified by the Japanese Society for Radiation Oncology. We used this database to evaluate the potential clinical benefits of PBT by comparing the NTCP calculated from the actual PBT and hypothetical photon radiation therapy in patients who underwent PBT for primary brain tumors.

The purpose of this in silico study was to compare the NTCP calculated from the PBT plans performed at participating centers (NTCPPBT) with the NTCP calculated from our hypothetical intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) plans (NTCPIMRT). The primary endpoints are NTCP calculated from the actual PBT plans and NTCP calculated from our virtual IMRT plans for each tumor group (meningioma, low-grade glioma, high-grade glioma, and glioblastoma). If the difference between NTCPPBT and NTCPIMRT (ΔNTCP = NTCPIMRT − NTCPPBT) exceeds a set threshold, PBT was considered to have a clinically meaningful reduction in the modeled NTCP, and the proportion of each case was calculated for each adverse event. A secondary endpoint is the research for factors that influence NTCP.

Eligible patients who initiated PBT between May 1, 2016, and April 30, 2021, at 13 participating institutions were registered in the Proton-net database and treated under a unified policy without expressing refusal to participate. Details on the policy are given in the supplementary material A.
Exclusion criteria were treatment with hyperfractionated irradiation, reirradiation, or a combination of photon radiation therapy and PBT.
This study was approved by the research ethics review committee of Hokkaido University Hospital (022-0263).

Clinical data, planning computed tomography images (<3 mm thickness), and magnetic resonance imaging sequences with thermoplastic masks were collected from participating institutions to generate virtual IMRT plans corresponding to each site’s clinical PBT plan.

We did not add any new organs at risk (OAR) for planning purposes because we used the same dose constraints in creating our virtual IMRT plans as the PBT plans. However, because doses were prescribed to the clinical target volume (CTV) in the PBT plans, the planning target volume (PTV) was created as CTV + 3 mm when creating the IMRT plan because the setup uncertainty was considered at 3 mm in the PBT plans. The treatment plan was created so that the same dose was prescribed to the CTV and PTV, respectively, as in the PBT plan, minimizing the dose to the OAR as far as possible. In other words, the IMRT plan was optimized so that the doses prescribed for 98%, 95%, 50%, and 2% of the target volume in the PBT plan were within 2% of those in the PBT plan. If it was difficult to achieve all dose prescriptions to the target volume, the treatment plan with the fewest deviations from the prescribed doses was selected. For patients with multiple PBT plans, corresponding virtual IMRT plans were generated. Medical physicists, blinded to the original PBT plans and provided only target doses and OAR constraints, generated all IMRT plans, followed by radiation oncologist approval. RayStation version 10.0 (RaySearch Laboratories) was used for treatment planning.

Table 1 shows the NTCP models selected.8,9,12, 13, 14, 15, 16 The selection of models was based on the selection criteria reported by Langendijk et al.17 If equivalent dose in 2 Gy fraction was required for the NTCP calculation, it was calculated as appropriate according to the Linear-Quadratic (LQ) model. For the models of excess absolute risk (EAR; EARCNS, EARSkin), we set the predicted age of onset for each tumor group because the expected prognosis depends on the grade of the tumor: meningiomas and low-grade gliomas were calculated as at 10 years after the radiation therapy, high-grade gliomas at 5 years, and glioblastomas at 2 years.

Most of the adverse events defined in the NTCP model were graded, but those not specified were graded by us based on the content of the paper15,16 and with reference to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0 to make them equivalent. Specifically, blindness was graded as grade 4, cataracts as grade 2, and delayed recall as equivalent to grade 1.

Additional OAR contours were created using an established atlas18 when necessary. For patients with multiple PBT plans, digital image registration to the most recent computed tomography was performed using MIM Maestro (MIM Software Inc) to generate the evaluation isodose line, using the boost plan’s target volume. This ensures optimal normal brain dose evaluation on the most recent anatomy. PBT NTCPs were calculated using nominal plan values. Endocrine dysfunction NTCP evaluation excluded 2 cases where tumors replaced the pituitary gland. The ipsilateral inner ear was defined by the higher mean PBT dose or, if equal, the primary lesion side. Bilateral hippocampi were combined into a single contour for evaluation.

We determined the threshold of ΔNTCP in accordance with previous studies as follows17: grade 1 was 20%, grade 2 was 10%, grade 3 was 5%, and grade 4 was 2% or more. If ΔNTCP of EAR was >0, PBT was considered favorable.

To observe factors associated with NTCP, the number and volume of tumor-occupied areas were measured. Occupied areas were defined as 9 areas in the left and right frontal lobes, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, occipital lobe, and occipital fossa, and in each case, the area where the tumor was present on the image was measured.

To objectively demonstrate the quality of the virtual IMRT plans, we audited their compliance with the OAR and planning organ at risk volume (PRV) dose constraints. The compliance rate for each OAR was calculated as the percentage of plans meeting the predefined criteria (strictly achieved or minor acceptable deviation), with the denominator restricted to the cases where that specific constraint had been applied in the original PBT plan. Furthermore, to evaluate the robustness of our clinical significance framework, we performed a sensitivity analysis using a unified threshold of ΔNTCP ≥ 2% for late CNS effects (blindness, brain necrosis, delayed recall, and memory impairment), as even small differences in these endpoints can be clinically critical.

The NTCPs for all patients were calculated for PBT and IMRT, respectively, for each adverse event, and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test was performed for statistically significant differences between the 2 modalities for patients overall and for tumor subtypes. A 2-tailed test was considered significant at a significance level of <.05. Statistical analysis was performed using JMP Pro 17 (SAS Institute Inc).

Given the numerous endpoints evaluated and the small sample sizes in certain histologic subgroups (eg, low-grade glioma, n = 6), all subgroup analyses were explicitly framed as exploratory. To address the risk of multiplicity, no formal adjustments for multiple comparisons were applied. Therefore, P values for subgroup analyses should be interpreted with caution. For these small subgroups, we shifted the analytical emphasis from definitive P values to effect sizes and their uncertainty, focusing on the median paired differences (ΔNTCP) and IQRs.
The RATING score was 96%, and the score sheet showing the results is attached as a supplementary file.

Table 2 contains characteristics of 66 patients. Of all patients, 59 (89.4%) had a diagnosis confirmed by histopathology, whereas the others had a clinical diagnosis. The histologic type of tumor was based on the 2016 edition of the CNS WHO classification because the patients were treated until 2021. The histologic types were glioblastoma (21 patients), glioma (17 patients), and meningioma (28 patients). There were no significant differences in CTV volume (P = .3863) or number of occupied areas (P = .4551) between the subgroups by histologic type.

We generated 119 virtual IMRT plans matching the PBT plans using the TrueBeam radiation therapy system (Varian Medical Systems). Overall, 84 (70.6%) and 105 (88.2%) IMRT plans achieved within ±2% and ±3% of the PBT target dose, respectively. Among 984 individual dose restrictions, 94.6% and 97.6% were within ±2% and ±3% deviations, respectively. The OAR-specific audit showed >96% clinical compliance (strict achievement plus minor deviations) for most critical OARs (eg, brainstem, optic nerves, and chiasm). Whole-brain compliance was 83.9%, reflecting IMRT’s low-dose spread (Supplementary material C). The baseline configuration was 6 MV beams with 2 planar/3 arcs. To meet strict constraints, arcs were increased in 5 plans (4.2%, up to 5 arcs). No plan required an unfeasible number of arcs, ensuring that all plans remained clinically deliverable.
A typical case of IMRT planning is given in the supplementary file.

Table 3 shows NTCPPBT and NTCPIMRT for each of the 4 groups classified by histopathology. For all patients, NTCPPBT was significantly lower than NTCPIMRT for cataracts, delayed recall, contralateral hearing impairment, tinnitus, and memory impairment. Notably, PBT had a lower NTCP of EARCNS than IMRT. In contrast, IMRT had significantly lower NTCP for alopecia, blindness, and brain necrosis than PBT.

When analyzed by histologic type, in meningioma, high-grade glioma, and glioblastoma, NTCPPBT for contralateral hearing impairment and tinnitus, memory impairment was lower than NTCPIMRT. In meningioma and high-grade glioma, NTCPPBT for delayed recall was lower than NTCPIMRT. All these differences are statistically significant (P < .05).

To physically substantiate these NTCP findings, a direct comparison of OAR dose metrics was performed. As detailed in Supplementary material D, PBT significantly reduced doses to the bilateral hippocampi, brain-CTV, and lenses compared with IMRT, while resulting in higher doses to the skin and brain-gross tumor volume (GTV). These dosimetric differences were entirely consistent with the observed trends in NTCP for each endpoint.

To visually summarize these dosimetric trade-offs, a benefit-tradeoff map was constructed (Fig. 1). This forest plot illustrates the median paired dose differences between the virtual IMRT and the PBT plans. As clearly depicted, PBT demonstrated a substantial dosimetric advantage in sparing structures such as the bilateral hippocampi, lenses, and contralateral cochlea (plotted on the right), whereas IMRT showed better sparing of the skin and brain-GTV (plotted on the left).

Table 4A shows the ratio of cases in each pathology in which the ΔNTCP exceeded the threshold, so PBT was found to be more beneficial than IMRT. Delayed recall, cataract, and memory impairment were associated with a higher percentage of benefit from PBT, in that order, with each adverse event being observed in more than 10% of all cases. PBT was useful in at least 1 or more of the NTCPs in 31 patients (47.0%).

We examined whether there was an association between the ΔNTCP and patient characteristics. The ΔNTCP of contralateral hearing impairment (P = .0064) and memory impairment (P < .0001) was greater when CTV volume was greater than the median (99.1 mL), and the ΔNTCP of memory impairment was greater when the occipital lobe was involved (P = .0237). There was no significant association between ΔNTCP and the number of regions (1 vs >1), presence of lesions in the frontal, temporal, or parietal lobes, or irradiation method.

sections.title: Sensitivity analysis with a unified threshold for CNS effects

paragraphs.en: To evaluate the robustness of our clinical significance framework, we performed an exploratory sensitivity analysis using a unified threshold of ΔNTCP ≥ 2% for late CNS effects (blindness, brain necrosis, delayed recall, and memory impairment), as even small differences in these endpoints can be clinically critical (Table 4B). Under this scenario, 77.3% of patients had at least 1 endpoint favoring PBT. This analysis should not be interpreted as establishing clinical superiority, but rather as illustrating how the estimated proportion of patients potentially benefiting from PBT depends on the selected ΔNTCP threshold.

In this study, we conducted a highly objective comparison using the existing NTCP model in a model-based approach and evaluated the usefulness of PBT with RATING. To our knowledge, this is the first study to use a model-based approach using NTCP that took on this objective measure.

We kept the prescription dose for the target volume and constraints of the OAR in the PBT plans, created virtual IMRT plans, and made a rigorous NTCP comparison. Dutz et al19 found that at least 95% of the PTV was greater than 95% of the prescribed dose (V95% > 95%) and that 2% was <107%, and all of our IMRT plans also met at least 2 of the 4 target volume dose constraints. With these conditions, most IMRT plans were able to achieve tight dose constraints, which is a new approach for planning studies to approximate the dose-volume histogram curve as closely as possible.

The most significant result of this study was that the EAR of second cancers of the CNS was significantly lower with PBT than with IMRT in all patients, not in any specific subpopulation. Because secondary cancers typically manifest at least 10 years after radiation therapy, PBT-mediated risk reduction is highly relevant for younger patients with long expected survival, where the 5-year relative survival for nonmalignant tumors reaches 96.5%.20 Conversely, for patients with short expected prognoses, such as glioblastoma (median survival: 8 months20), the clinical benefit of PBT over IMRT diminishes despite lower calculated NTCPs.

PBT partially reduced the other NTCP compared with IMRT. Our results suggest that PBT may be particularly advantageous for sparing contralateral organs and normal tissues for which low-dose exposure is clinically relevant. This result agrees with previous studies demonstrating the usefulness of PBT; Dutz et al19 validated the eligibility of PBT using 11 NTCP models. The results showed that ΔNTCP improved in 80 of 92 cases, indicating the effectiveness of PBT. Langendijk et al17 argued for the need to change the threshold of ΔNTCP according to grading by the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events. Furthermore, we addressed the potential clinical impact of small absolute differences in CNS-related endpoints, particularly cognition. Although our primary analysis followed a standard grading-based threshold, we conducted a sensitivity analysis applying a lower threshold (ΔNTCP ≥ 2%) for late CNS toxicities. This additional analysis suggests the potential clinical benefit of PBT in protecting delicate CNS tissues, where even minor dose reductions may result in meaningful preservation of patient quality of life.

NTCP for alopecia, blindness, and brain necrosis was significantly lower with IMRT than with PBT. The reason that NTCP of alopecia is higher in PBT than IMRT may be because of the absence of the buildup seen with x-ray therapy. For blindness, only 9.1% (1/11) of patients treated with the spot-scanning method had a higher NTCP of blindness than that of IMRT, suggesting that differences in irradiation methods may have an influence on NTCP of blindness. For brain necrosis, the generalized equivalent uniform dose of the brain-GTV, which is required for NTCP calculation, is highly influenced by the extent of the high-dose region; a broader high-dose region results in a higher generalized equivalent uniform dose. In PBT plans, the proximal and distal margins of 3.5% of the respective beam ranges are added to account for range uncertainty. Consequently, the high-dose region tends to extend farther proximally and distally than in IMRT, which may account for the higher NTCP for brain necrosis observed with PBT. Because 83.3% of our cohort was treated with broad beam irradiation, the present findings may not fully reflect contemporary pencil beam scanning (PBS)-based practice. PBS allows for superior proximal dose reduction and more conformal dose distributions than broad beam method; therefore, it may alter the balance of benefits and trade-offs, particularly for skin dose and high-dose brain exposure. However, this requires validation in a larger PBS cohort.

As an exploration of factors related to ΔNTCP, it was suggested that PBT may be beneficial when tumor volume is large. Although Adeberg et al20 related PBT efficacy to tumor center location, we classified sites by area of occupancy to better account for variations in tumor size and morphology relative to OARs. Consequently, a significant ΔNTCP difference was observed only for memory impairment in occipital lobe lesions. Compared with Dutz et al,19 our cohort had a higher proportion of multilobe lesions (56.1% vs 33.7%), potentially placing targets closer to OARs and reducing PBT-mediated dose sparing.

First, half of the cohort of NTCP models used in this comparison is x-ray-based, and the other half is PBT-based, but there may be some uncertainty involved when using a different modality in the NTCP model than the modality on which the model is based. This is because of the difference in the evaluation method of the target volume: PTV is used for x-ray therapy, whereas robust evaluation is used for the PBT. It has also been suggested that relative biological effectiveness (RBE) is higher at the distal end of the Bragg peak in PBT, further complicating the relationship between modalities. Because our study used nominal doses based on a constant RBE of 1.1, the true biological dose at the distal edge may be underestimated. This could lead to discrepancies in endpoints closely related to high-dose regions, such as brain necrosis. To resolve these issues, an NTCP model with variable RBE (eg, the McNamara model) is needed.

Second, the overall sample size was small, and specific histology subgroups were particularly underpowered (eg, low-grade glioma, n = 6 and high-grade glioma, n = 11). Because we evaluated multiple endpoints without formal adjustments for multiple comparisons, our subgroup findings must be interpreted strictly as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Consequently, we avoided drawing definitive clinical conclusions for these small subpopulations, emphasizing effect sizes and IQRs rather than relying solely on P values to guide our interpretations.

Third, this study may present selection bias because PBT for brain tumors is not covered by national health care insurance in Japan. This bias may have an impact on patient outcomes; however, it is considered to have little effect on the predicted difference in NTCP between PBT and IMRT.

Fourth, our virtual IMRT plans were generated at a single institution. Although the planning was conducted by experienced medical physicists who were blinded to the original PBT dose distributions and adhered to strict OAR constraints, treatment planning is inherently sensitive to individual planner decisions. The lack of a multiplanner reproducibility check or benchmarking against real-world clinical IMRT plans for this specific cohort remains a limitation that could introduce planning bias.

This study used multiple NTCP models in accordance with RATING and suggested that PBT was associated with lower NTCPs for selected endpoints compared with IMRT. PBT appears to be advantageous in sparing contralateral organs and structures for which low-dose exposure is clinically relevant. Furthermore, it shows the potential to reduce the risk of secondary cancer, especially in young patients and in disease groups with long expected survival. To further substantiate the benefits of PBT, NTCP models based on PBT-treated patients and external validation of existing models are needed.

sections.title: Declaration of Generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the writing process

paragraphs.en: During the preparation of this work the authors used ChatGPT in order to language translation and proofreading. After using this tool, the authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the publication.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Benefit-tradeoff map comparing dosimetric outcomes of virtual IMRT and PBT. The plot displays median paired dose differences (IMRT −PBT) for key OARs, with error bars representing IQR. Points to the right of the red dashed line (difference >0) indicate lower metrics with PBT (favoring PBT); points to the left (difference <0) indicate lower metrics with virtual IMRT (favoring IMRT). Because endpoints include both dose-based (Gy[RBE]) and volume-based (%) metrics, horizontal magnitudes should not be compared directly across different OARs. This summarizes the direction and distribution of modality-related differences for each NTCP model input.Abbreviations: CTV = clinical target volume; gEUD = generalized equivalent uniform dose; IMRT = intensity modulated radiation therapy; NTCP = normal tissue complication probability; OAR = organs at risk; PBT = proton beam therapy; RBE = relative biological effectiveness.
